Fig1_Polynya_source_footprint: The left panel maps eighty-five sampled Adélie colony sites along the Antarctic coast. Marker colours run from dark purple for a smaller average share of ocean in coastal polynyas to yellow for a larger share. The averages use June through October. Thin circles mark the sampling area within one hundred kilometres of each colony. Pale land shows the coastline for orientation. Letter labels link map locations to the table on the right, which counts sites and colony-seasons in eleven regions. The counts vary across regions and total four hundred thirty-nine colony-seasons from winters beginning in two thousand four through two thousand ten.
Fig2_Polynya_association_and_sensitivity: The upper plot shows estimated differences in the optical nitrogen isotope proxy, in parts per thousand per ten percentage points of winter polynya cover. Four rows compare the same images under original and alternative calibrations, each with and without adjusting for summer salinity. Filled markers show jackknife intervals calculated by leaving out one region at a time. Hollow grey markers show the earlier region-cluster intervals. All four jackknife intervals lie left of zero. Below, circles show estimates without salinity adjustment and squares show estimates with it. Both estimates stay negative when any one of the eleven reporting regions is left out. The lower plot shows point estimates only.
Fig3_Preceding_following_winter_contrast: The top timeline places the summer optical nitrogen isotope proxy between the preceding and following winters for three hundred fifty-eight matched colony-seasons. Below, the first two rows show the winter coefficients estimated in the same model. The next two subtract the following-winter coefficient from the preceding-winter coefficient, using each proxy calibration. The horizontal axis gives parts per thousand per ten percentage points of polynya cover. Filled markers show jackknife intervals calculated by leaving out one region at a time. Hollow grey markers show the earlier region-cluster intervals. Both difference estimates are negative. The earlier intervals end just below zero, but both jackknife intervals include zero, leaving the timing difference uncertain.
Fig4_Polynya_salinity_conditional_inform: The left scatter plot shows deviations in winter polynya cover across the horizontal axis and deviations in summer surface salinity up the vertical axis. The points cluster near zero after accounting for colony and conditions shared within each region and season. Across four hundred thirty-nine observations, the correlation is minus zero point zero eight zero four three. On the right, horizontal bars show how much less variation remains unexplained when salinity, polynya cover or both are added to the same baseline model. The reductions are two point one four, three point seven nine and five point two nine percent, respectively. Whether the two exposures act independently remains unresolved.
Fig5_Observation_and_unresolved_pathways: At the top, a solid line without an arrow links greater winter polynya cover to a lower summer optical nitrogen isotope proxy within colonies. In the middle, dashed arrows show three possible explanations: prey composition, prey isotope baselines, and changes in the surface or mixture contributing to guano reflectance. These pathways remain unresolved. In the shaded bottom panel, Reaves and colleagues compared modern and ancient chick bones across fifteen colony locations. The panel links southern latent-heat polynya settings with higher chick-bone nitrogen isotope values in southern colonies. This spatial comparison spans different colonies and timescales and leaves the annual polynya-area relationship within colonies untested.
